system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 14 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2170-12-17 00:33:00 to 2170-12-30 14:25:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with idiopathic chronic pancreatitis was admitted with abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting consistent with a flare. She was managed with bowel rest, IV fluids, and pain control using IV hydromorphone, which was later transitioned to oral medications. A chest X-ray and fluoroscopic evaluation confirmed the PICC line was in satisfactory position for TPN, so no repositioning was needed. The pain service recommended increasing gabapentin, which was initiated at 600 mg nightly with a plan for outpatient uptitration. She gradually improved, tolerated oral intake, and was discharged home with TPN, a stable PICC line, and follow-up plans with her gastroenterologist for medication management and nutritional support.
problems: Family history of malignant neoplasm of gastrointestinal tract

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you're here with abdominal pain and nausea again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s the same pain I had before—right in the upper belly. It came back hard just a day after I left the hospital last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were discharged about 36 hours ago, and the pain and vomiting returned despite your usual medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. I took Compazine, Zofran, and Dilaudid, but nothing helped. I knew I had to come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did the right thing. We’ll keep you on bowel rest again and give you IV fluids and pain control. We’ve started you on IV Dilaudid and Zofran for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on TPN again? I remember that helped last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart TPN through your PICC line. We checked a chest X-ray early this morning, and your line is still in good position—tip in the upper vena cava.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good, I was worried it might have moved. My mom had pancreatic cancer—do we need to rule that out again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand your concern. Your labs don’t show signs of infection or severe inflammation. Lipase is only mildly elevated. This looks like a flare of your chronic pancreatitis, not a new issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. But the pain is so hard to control. Last time, the PCA made me too sleepy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re avoiding the PCA this time. You’ll get IV Dilaudid as needed, and we’ve asked the pain service to help optimize your regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your TPN was started yesterday, and labs are stable. The pain service met with you—they recommend starting amitriptyline at night and increasing gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Amitriptyline? Isn’t that for depression?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can help with nerve-related pain, especially in chronic pancreatitis. Since you’re already on sertraline and bupropion, this is more for pain than mood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. And gabapentin—I was only taking it at night before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll increase it to three times a day. The goal is to reduce nerve hypersensitivity that contributes to your pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Will I stay on TPN the whole time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. We’ll wait until your pain is better and then slowly reintroduce clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain seems a bit better today. How would you rate it now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe a 6 out of 10, down from 9. The new gabapentin dose helps, especially at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep building on that. We’re also lowering your IV Dilaudid as you tolerate oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try some water or broth soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with ice chips and clear liquids today, if your nausea stays under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been doing well on clear liquids. Any nausea or pain with drinking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just mild discomfort, no vomiting. I’m glad the TPN is helping my body rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep advancing your diet slowly. We also ordered an MRCP to check for any changes in your pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that an MRI? I’ve had a few of those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a special MRI that looks at the pancreas and bile ducts. We want to make sure there are no new complications like pseudocysts or blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRCP results are back. Good news—your pancreas looks stable. No new masses, fluid collections, or duct blockages. It’s still consistent with chronic changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Any other findings?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There are some small stable liver nodules and a renal cyst, all unchanged. Also, they saw large perineural cysts in your pelvis—likely old and not causing symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, nothing urgent then. My pain is down to a 4 now with oral Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll keep you on the fentanyl patch, gabapentin, and amitriptyline. You’re doing well with oral pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been off IV meds for two days and tolerating a soft diet. We’re planning for discharge in a few days if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Will I still need TPN at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for now. You’ll continue TPN at home and slowly transition to more oral intake. Your GI doctor will help taper it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds—will they change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll start gabapentin 600 mg three times daily and amitriptyline 10 mg at night. We’re also adjusting your Dilaudid to 2 mg tablets for better control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was taking 8 mg before. Is 2 mg enough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have up to four doses a day, so 8 mg max. But we’re starting lower since your pain is better and to reduce side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about my omeprazole? I was on 40 mg twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reducing it to 20 mg twice daily. It’s still important for reflux, but we’re adjusting based on your current needs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your bladder? Still using tolterodine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it helps. I know it’s not the main issue, but it’s good to have some control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it. Also, your labs show mild anemia, but it’s stable—consistent with chronic disease, not new bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s been my baseline for years. My hemoglobin was 9.3 on admission, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and it’s now 8.4. A slight drop, but not concerning. We’re not planning transfusions—just monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re walking daily, eating well, and pain is manageable. We’re on track for discharge tomorrow or the next day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Will I have help with TPN?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll go home with visiting nurses to assist with TPN and check your PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final plan: discharge tomorrow morning. You’ll follow up with Dr. ___ in one week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my pain flares again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your oral meds as prescribed. If no relief in 24 hours, or if you can’t keep fluids down, come back or call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my son? He has a CF gene mutation. Should he be screened for pancreas issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good question. Heterozygous CF mutations increase risk slightly, but not as much as full CF. Discuss with his doctor about monitoring, especially if he has symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge today. Your pain is controlled, you’re eating, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take the new meds as directed. Gabapentin three times, amitriptyline at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep using omeprazole, ondansetron for nausea, and your bladder meds. TPN continues as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll see my GI doctor in a week and call if anything worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’ve worked hard to get through this flare. Take it easy at home and keep building your strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before you leave. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. Thank you for helping me through this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with idiopathic chronic pancreatitis was readmitted within 36 hours of discharge due to recurrent abdominal pain and nausea, consistent with a flare. She was managed with bowel rest, TPN via her stable PICC line, IV hydromorphone initially, and antiemetics. The pain service recommended increasing gabapentin to three times daily and starting amitriptyline at night for neuropathic pain. Her symptoms gradually improved, allowing transition to oral pain medications and advancement to a soft diet. An MRCP showed stable chronic pancreatitis without acute complications. She was discharged home on TPN with visiting nurse support, new prescriptions for gabapentin and amitriptyline, and a follow-up appointment with her gastroenterologist in one week.
